Cerebras Sinks 11% in a Week to a New 52-Week Low. UBS Still Sees 159% Upside ©@wooyaa from Getty Images via Canva, @AndreyPopov from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Cerebras stock fell 11% in the past week to a new 52-week low, 75% below its May high.

Oracle will offer Cerebras' inference on its cloud, but a short seller and Oracle's $20 billion raise outweighed the deal.

The main risk is Culper Research's claim that Cerebras' wafers break down after about two years, which Cerebras hasn't answered.

UBS cut its target to $250 but kept its Buy, and the Nov. 12 report is the next test.

Cerebras Systems (CBRS:NASDAQ) stock is down 11% in the past week. It closed Monday at a new 52-week low, 75% below its May 14 high.

That happened even though the business got good news: on Oct. 27, Cerebras and Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) said Oracle Cloud Infrastructure will offer Cerebras' fast inference. A short seller and Oracle's own funding needs did the damage.

Oracle opened a new door

Oracle said that day it's expanding its Nvidia chip deals while adding rivals such as Google and Cerebras. So Cerebras now sits on a major AI cloud beside the incumbent, as analysts expect its revenue to more than triple next year:

Cerebras Systems (CBRS): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2026-2029 (TIKR)
A short seller's two-year claim

The next day, Culper Research said on X it's short the stock, and that "$CBRS wafers break down after just ~2 years in use – a lifespan that undermines the entire business."

If that's true, customers would replace Cerebras hardware sooner than planned, raising what each year of computing costs them.

Culper's figure is unproven so far. But Cerebras hasn't answered it publicly.

Its new partner's $20 billion raise

Cerebras had no news of its own on Monday. Oracle filed before the open to raise $20 billion in stock and bonds for its AI buildout. Oracle fell 9%, and AI infrastructure stocks fell with it.

Cerebras' newest sales channel depends on that buildout.

TIKR tracks 11 analysts on Cerebras Systems. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Cerebras Systems, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Cerebras Systems' Analyst Ratings

The Street hasn't budged

That morning, UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri cut his target to $250 from $330 and kept his Buy. That's 159% above Monday's close.

At $250, the stock would trade at around 41x forward sales. At Monday's close it traded at 16x, its lowest since listing and less than half its 36x average:

Cerebras Systems (CBRS): forward (NTM) price/sales, since it listed (TIKR)

The consensus target from 11 analysts has barely moved, from $294 in June to $275 now:

Cerebras Systems (CBRS): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, since it listed (TIKR)
What the report has to show

Cerebras reports third-quarter results after the close on Thursday, Nov. 12. It needs to answer Culper on wafer life, show early Oracle demand, and keep next year's estimates in reach.

Key Takeaways

CoreWeave rose 5% and Oracle 4% after Oracle priced a $20 billion sale of stock and bonds.

Oracle's deal shows lenders still fund AI builders, which matters most to CoreWeave, a far costlier borrower.

AMD, Super Micro and Cipher Digital rose too.

CoreWeave reports Nov. 10, with third-quarter interest expense guided well above adjusted operating income.

CoreWeave (CRWV:NASDAQ) jumped 5% today, and Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) rose 4%, after Oracle priced $20 billion of new stock and bonds late Monday.

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) rose 4% and Super Micro Computer (SMCI:NASDAQ) 4%, and Cipher Digital (CIFR:NASDAQ) jumped 16%.

Exactly what Oracle said it would do

Oracle is selling 86.2 million shares at $116 apiece, plus $10 billion of notes with coupons of 7% to 8.65%. That fits the roughly $40 billion it said in June it would raise in fiscal 2027.

Baird analyst Rob Oliver said the sale "seems to be exactly what they previewed."

CoreWeave pays a lot more for its money

Analysts expect CoreWeave's revenue to climb from $5.13 billion in 2025 to $26.5 billion in 2027:

CoreWeave (CRWV): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2025-2028 (TIKR)

Oracle's raise shouldn't move those estimates, but CoreWeave must borrow to hit them: consensus sees negative free cash flow every year through 2030.

And it pays more than Oracle does. Its last two unsecured bond deals came at 9.75% in April and 9.625% in June, and its 9.625% notes due 2032 traded at a yield near 15% in mid-October.

The stock trades like investors doubt it will get that money. CoreWeave closed Monday at 1.4x forward sales, its low for the past year and well under its 3.6x average:

CoreWeave (CRWV): forward (NTM) price/sales, last year (TIKR)
The suppliers report tonight

AMD supplies the MI450 chips for Oracle's planned 50,000-GPU cluster. Super Micro agreed this morning to build SambaNova inference racks, starting with 10,000 chips. Their reports tonight will show whether money like Oracle's is still turning into orders.

After Cipher's third-quarter report Monday, JPMorgan cut its target to $18 from $22. Cipher needs tenants to keep signing leases, and Keefe, Bruyette & Woods warned that new ones could dry up.

We just published the list of the 10 Best and Cheap Stocks to Buy Heading into 2027 and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) ranks 6th on this list.

Wall Street's AI trade took a hard hit on October 30. Reuters reported that a selloff in tech shares pushed MSCI's global index down 1.5%, after results from Intel and Amazon showed how much cash AI spending is burning. Intel fell 28.6%, and the Philadelphia semiconductor index lost more than 7%, its biggest one-day drop since late June. Alphabet's shares had already slid 12.6% a day earlier, after it reported that its AI spending pushed its cash flow negative.

The nervousness had been building. Reuters reported on October 15 that South Korea's KOSPI index, home to some of the world's largest chipmakers, fell roughly 8% in a single session. Saxo Bank chief investment strategist Charu Chanana said the Asian selloff looked less like a sudden deterioration in technology fundamentals and more like a repricing of the cost of capital.

READ ALSO 10 Best Robotics Stocks to Buy That Are More Than 30% On Sale

Rates are a large part of that story. Bloomberg reported on October 4 that benchmark 10-year Treasury yields sat near 5.3%, and Franklin Templeton Institute head market strategist Chris Galipeau said the conversation would change if they reached 6%. Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Robert Schiffman added that hyperscalers such as Meta, Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft and Oracle now have cash needs far beyond what they generate, which pushes them toward debt markets.

Oracle made our list of the best and cheap stocks to buy for two reasons. First, its forward P/E is 11 and expected revenue growth rate for 2027 is nearly 32%. Second, it is one of the most popular stocks among hedge funds which is why ORCL is one of the best cheap stocks to buy according to hedge funds.

Oracle's investor day gave the market something it had been missing: dates. Chief financial officer Hilary Maxson said free cash flow is expected to turn positive in the second half of fiscal 2028 and reach at least $30 billion in fiscal 2029, far above what Wall Street had been expecting, according to data compiled by Bloomberg and FactSet. Capital spending is expected to peak in fiscal 2027 and 2028 before easing, and Oracle said growth is expected to become self-funded once it does.

Is Oracle’s (ORCL) Massive Bet Finally About to Pay Off?

Management also capped new fundraising through fiscal 2030 at $20 billion, split evenly between stock and debt, which answered the worry that the AI buildout would keep demanding outside money. Oracle reaffirmed its goal of at least $225 billion in fiscal 2030 revenue and pointed to $664 billion of contracted future revenue behind it.

Quantinuum Inc. QNT is scheduled to report its third-quarter 2026 results on Nov. 5, after market close. The quantum computing company is heading into its second earnings announcement as a public company amid a steep decline in its share price and weakening investor sentiment toward pure-play quantum computing stocks.

Since the beginning of July, QNT shares have plunged 38.7%, significantly underperforming the Internet Software Market, which advanced 16.4% and the S&P 500 index, which gained 1.7%, according to the supplied Zacks price-performance data.

July-September QNT Stock Performance
Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

What Do Q3 Earnings Estimates for QNT Say?

The Zacks Consensus Estimate for Quantinuum's third-quarter 2026 revenues is pegged at $8.15 million, based on three analyst estimates. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for third-quarter bottom line is pegged at a loss of 38 cents per share, based on four analyst estimates.

The company reported second-quarter revenues of $8 million, reflecting 279% year-over-year growth. Adjusted net loss per share was 28 cents. The third-quarter consensus estimates therefore indicate modest revenue growth and a widening adjusted loss per share sequentially.

Quantinuum Inc. Price and EPS Surprise
Quantinuum Inc. Price and EPS Surprise

Quantinuum Inc. price-eps-surprise | Quantinuum Inc. Quote

Strategic Progress Fails to Lift QNT Stock Amid Broader Quantum Selloff

The stock's weakness during July to September was particularly notable considering Quantinuum's strategic developments since its June 2026 initial public offering (IPO). The company announced a major partnership with Oracle ORCL, strengthened its manufacturing ecosystem through a collaboration with Quanta Computer and finalized a $100 million award agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce's CHIPS Research and Development Office. It also reported encouraging technological progress on its Helios quantum computer and continued advancing its next-generation Sol system.

However, Quantinuum is not alone in facing investor skepticism. Other pure-play quantum computing companies, including IonQ IONQ and D-Wave Quantum QBTS, have also struggled to sustain their share-price momentum despite significant commercial and technological developments. IonQ's revenue growth, expanded strategic partnerships and progress on its next-generation quantum systems are yet to fully offset concerns about its substantial operating losses and commercialization timelines. Similarly, D-Wave's strong bookings growth and government-backed initiatives have not insulated its shares from the broader sector correction.

On Monday, three of the biggest AI spenders came to the bond market at once. Our unofficial count of the deals reaches at least $36.7 billion.

Stas_V / Getty Images

Only $16.7 billion of that was priced. Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG, NASDAQ:GOOGL) and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) completed their sales, while Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) only began sounding out investors.

Oracle fell 8.85% on Monday, a drop tied to its own stock and bond filing. Meta slipped 1.34% to $606.73, and Alphabet eased 0.30% to $278.99. Lenders priced the three very differently, and the terms show which can fund an AI build cheaply.

What Priced Monday and What Is Still Just Talk

Alphabet sold €6 billion, about $6.7 billion, in seven tranches: one floating-rate note and six fixed-rate notes. Orders passed €17 billion, coupons ran from 3.700% to 5.250%, and the deal settles November 5.

Oracle priced $10 billion in five fixed-rate tranches with coupons from 7.000% to 8.650%, settling November 4. On the same day, it filed to sell $10 billion of common stock. That sale is equity, so it stays out of the bond count.

Meta has not priced or confirmed its deal. The reported floor is $20 billion, possibly split into 5 dollar and 6 euro tranches, and Meta's SEC filings showed no prospectus dated Monday.

title: Hyperscalers Face “$1.5 Trillion Gap” Between AI Spending and Cash
detail:
Hyperscalers Face “$1.5 Trillion Gap” Between AI Spending and Cash
Roxanna Maglangit

Hyperscalers Face "$1.5 Trillion Gap" Between AI Spending and Cash ©Natee Meepian's Images and Yuganov Konstantin via Canva
Key Takeaways

Hyperscaler free cash flow turned negative in the third quarter for the first time, and Microsoft is the only one of Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Oracle with positive free cash flow.

Prof G Markets co-host Ed Elson expects the five companies to spend more than $2 trillion on capex over the next two years, against nearly $600 billion of cash on hand.

His $1.5 trillion figure leaves out the cash these companies' operations still bring in, but spending is growing much faster than that cash, and Meta and Alphabet are already turning to stock and bond buyers.

Microsoft still pays for its buildout from operations, so it's the best placed of the five if investors get less willing to fund the rest.

Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ), Alphabet (GOOG), Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ), Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) and Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) are spending so much on AI data centers that, as a group, they can no longer pay for it out of their own cash flow.

Carson Group's Ryan Detrick flagged it on X on Monday, citing his colleague Sonu Varghese: "Hyperscaler free cash flow turned negative for the first time ever in Q3."

On Monday's episode of Prof G Markets, co-host Ed Elson put a dollar figure on what that means. He expects the five companies' capex over the next two years to be more than $2 trillion. He counts nearly $600 billion of cash and short-term investments among them, including more than $120 billion at Amazon and more than $250 billion at Alphabet. That leaves, in his words, "a one and a half trillion dollar gap between how much money they're going to spend and how much money they actually have."

That's a lot of money to ask investors for.

TIKR tracks 57 analysts on Microsoft. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Microsoft, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Microsoft's Analyst Ratings

Smaller than $1.5 trillion, and growing fast

Elson's math leaves out one big thing: the cash these businesses still bring in from operations, which pays for most of the spending today. Negative free cash flow means the spending has moved ahead of that cash. The cash is still coming in.

Meta shows it clearly. Its capex has climbed until, in the September quarter, it was more than the cash its operations brought in:

Meta Platforms (META): cash from operations vs. capital expenditures, $ billions, last 8 quarters (to September 30, 2026) (TIKR)

Meta's capex rose 80% from a year earlier, to $33.9 billion, while its operating cash rose 9%, to $32.8 billion. That's the real gap, and it grows every quarter that spending rises faster than cash. Elson expects capex to keep rising next year and the year after, so the gap could get big quickly. By his count, Oracle, Amazon and Alphabet are already in negative free cash flow too.
